claim: Mto1, together with partner protein Mto2 (Mto1/2 complex), recruits the γ-tubulin complex to multiple non-centrosomal MTOCs, including the nuclear envelope (NE).
source: In fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe, the protein Mto1, together with partner protein Mto2 (Mto1/2 complex), recruits the γ-tubulin complex to multiple non-centrosomal MTOCs, including the nuclear envelope (NE).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about the Mto1/2 complex function.

claim: Mto1 is a constitutively cytoplasmic protein.
source: Surprisingly, we find that Mto1, a constitutively cytoplasmic protein, docks at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), via interaction with exportin Crm1 and cytoplasmic FG-nucleoporin Nup146.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a finding of the study.

claim: Mto1 docks at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) via interaction with exportin Crm1 and cytoplasmic FG-nucleoporin Nup146.
source: Surprisingly, we find that Mto1, a constitutively cytoplasmic protein, docks at nuclear pore complexes (NPCs), via interaction with exportin Crm1 and cytoplasmic FG-nucleoporin Nup146.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry and microscopy data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mto1 is not a nuclear export cargo.
source: Although Mto1 is not a nuclear export cargo, it binds Crm1 via a nuclear export signal-like sequence, and docking requires both Ran in the GTP-bound state and Nup146 FG repeats.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental evidence showing Mto1 is never present in the nucleus.

claim: Mto1 binds Crm1 via a nuclear export signal-like sequence.
source: Although Mto1 is not a nuclear export cargo, it binds Crm1 via a nuclear export signal-like sequence, and docking requires both Ran in the GTP-bound state and Nup146 FG repeats.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by deletion analysis and mass spectrometry data in Figure 4.

claim: Mto1 docking at NPCs requires Ran in the GTP-bound state.
source: Although Mto1 is not a nuclear export cargo, it binds Crm1 via a nuclear export signal-like sequence, and docking requires both Ran in the GTP-bound state and Nup146 FG repeats.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with Ran mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mto1 docking at NPCs requires Nup146 FG repeats.
source: Although Mto1 is not a nuclear export cargo, it binds Crm1 via a nuclear export signal-like sequence, and docking requires both Ran in the GTP-bound state and Nup146 FG repeats.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experiments with Nup146 FG repeat deletions shown in Figure 6.

claim: Differentiated animal cells such as neurons, muscle, and epithelial cells have non-centrosomal MTOCs.
source: Examples include differentiated animal cells such as neurons (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015), muscle (Mogessie et al., 2015; Tassin et al., 1985), and epithelial cells (Wu and Akhmanova, 2017), and many higher plant cells (Masoud et al., 2013; Oda, 2015), as well as some single-celled eukaryotes, such as fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Chang and Martin, 2009; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Many higher plant cells have non-centrosomal MTOCs.
source: Examples include differentiated animal cells such as neurons (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015), muscle (Mogessie et al., 2015; Tassin et al., 1985), and epithelial cells (Wu and Akhmanova, 2017), and many higher plant cells (Masoud et al., 2013; Oda, 2015), as well as some single-celled eukaryotes, such as fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Chang and Martin, 2009; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe has non-centrosomal MTOCs.
source: Examples include differentiated animal cells such as neurons (Kapitein and Hoogenraad, 2015), muscle (Mogessie et al., 2015; Tassin et al., 1985), and epithelial cells (Wu and Akhmanova, 2017), and many higher plant cells (Masoud et al., 2013; Oda, 2015), as well as some single-celled eukaryotes, such as fission yeast Schizosaccharomyces pombe (Chang and Martin, 2009; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some non-centrosomal MTs are generated by nucleation-and-release from the centrosome, followed by minus-end stabilization and anchoring elsewhere in the cell.
source: Some non-centrosomal MTs are thought to be generated by nucleation-and-release from the centrosome, followed by minus-end stabilization and anchoring elsewhere in the cell (Bartolini and Gundersen, 2006; Sanchez and Feldman, 2017; Wu and Akhmanova, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In many cases, MTs are nucleated directly from non-centrosomal sites by the γ-tubulin complex.
source: However, in many cases, MTs are nucleated directly from non-centrosomal sites by the γ-tubulin complex, the primary microtubule-nucleation complex in eukaryotic cells (Kollman et al., 2011; Petry and Vale, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The γ-tubulin complex is the primary microtubule-nucleation complex in eukaryotic cells.
source: However, in many cases, MTs are nucleated directly from non-centrosomal sites by the γ-tubulin complex, the primary microtubule-nucleation complex in eukaryotic cells (Kollman et al., 2011; Petry and Vale, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Sites of non-centrosomal γ-tubulin complex recruitment include pre-existing microtubules, the Golgi apparatus, and the nuclear envelope.
source: Sites of non-centrosomal γ-tubulin complex recruitment include pre-existing microtubules themselves, as well as membrane-bound compartments such as the Golgi apparatus and the nuclear envelope (NE).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Recruitment of the γ-tubulin complex to pre-existing microtubules depends on the multi-subunit augmin complex in both animals and plants.
source: Recruitment of the γ-tubulin complex to pre-existing microtubules depends on the multi-subunit augmin complex, in both animals and plants (Goshima et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014; Sánchez-Huertas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Microtubule nucleation and organization by the Golgi apparatus is orchestrated largely by AKAP450.
source: Microtubule nucleation and organization by the Golgi apparatus is orchestrated largely by AKAP450, which recruits not only the γ-tubulin complex but also its activators, as well as MT minus-end stabilizers (Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: AKAP450 recruits the γ-tubulin complex, its activators, and MT minus-end stabilizers.
source: Microtubule nucleation and organization by the Golgi apparatus is orchestrated largely by AKAP450, which recruits not only the γ-tubulin complex but also its activators, as well as MT minus-end stabilizers (Rivero et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Combined recruitment of γ-tubulin complex and MT minus-end stabilizers/anchoring proteins is important for MTOC organization at the cell cortex in diverse types of epithelial cells.
source: Combined recruitment of γ-tubulin complex and MT minus-end stabilizers/anchoring proteins is also important for MTOC organization at the cell cortex in diverse types of epithelial cells (summarized in [Sanchez and Feldman, 2017; Wu and Akhmanova, 2017]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: MTOC formation at the NE remains poorly understood.
source: MTOC formation at the NE remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: The NE is an important MT nucleation site in muscle cells.
source: The NE is an important MT nucleation site both in muscle cells (Tassin et al., 1985) and in higher plants (Ambrose and Wasteneys, 2014; Masoud et al., 2013; Stoppin et al., 1994), as well as in fission yeast (Lynch et al., 2014; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The NE is an important MT nucleation site in higher plants.
source: The NE is an important MT nucleation site both in muscle cells (Tassin et al., 1985) and in higher plants (Ambrose and Wasteneys, 2014; Masoud et al., 2013; Stoppin et al., 1994), as well as in fission yeast (Lynch et al., 2014; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The NE is an important MT nucleation site in fission yeast.
source: The NE is an important MT nucleation site both in muscle cells (Tassin et al., 1985) and in higher plants (Ambrose and Wasteneys, 2014; Masoud et al., 2013; Stoppin et al., 1994), as well as in fission yeast (Lynch et al., 2014; Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In muscle, γ-tubulin complex components and associated proteins are redistributed from the centrosome to the NE during development/differentiation.
source: In muscle, γ-tubulin complex components and associated proteins are redistributed from the centrosome to the NE during development/differentiation, coincident with a decrease in centrosomal MT nucleation and large-scale changes in intracellular MT organization (Bugnard et al., 2005; Fant et al., 2009; Srsen et al., 2009; Zebrowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Redistribution of γ-tubulin complex components to the NE in muscle is coincident with a decrease in centrosomal MT nucleation and large-scale changes in intracellular MT organization.
source: In muscle, γ-tubulin complex components and associated proteins are redistributed from the centrosome to the NE during development/differentiation, coincident with a decrease in centrosomal MT nucleation and large-scale changes in intracellular MT organization (Bugnard et al., 2005; Fant et al., 2009; Srsen et al., 2009; Zebrowski et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: In plant cells, which lack centrosomes, many of the same proteins are observed on the NE, especially before and/or after cell division.
source: In plant cells, which lack centrosomes altogether, many of the same proteins are similarly observed on the NE, especially before and/or after cell division (Erhardt et al., 2002; Janski et al., 2012; Nakamura et al., 2012; Seltzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Plant cells lack centrosomes.
source: In plant cells, which lack centrosomes altogether, many of the same proteins are similarly observed on the NE, especially before and/or after cell division (Erhardt et al., 2002; Janski et al., 2012; Nakamura et al., 2012; Seltzer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The mechanisms that regulate recruitment of γ-tubulin complex components to the NE are largely a mystery.
source: However, the mechanisms that regulate their recruitment are largely a mystery.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a knowledge gap.

claim: Fission yeast nucleate MTs from multiple non-centrosomal sites through the cell cycle.
source: Fission yeast nucleate MTs from multiple non-centrosomal sites through the cell cycle and thus provide an excellent system to study non-centrosomal MTOCs, including those on the NE (Sawin and Tran, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: During interphase, fission yeast linear arrays of MTs are nucleated from the spindle pole body (SPB), from MTOCs on the NE and on pre-existing microtubules, and from 'free' MTOCs in the cytoplasm.
source: During interphase, linear arrays of MTs are nucleated from the spindle pole body (SPB; the yeast centrosome equivalent), from MTOCs on the NE and on pre-existing microtubules, and from 'free' MTOCs in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about fission yeast.

claim: As fission yeast cells enter mitosis, non-centrosomal MT nucleation is switched off.
source: As cells enter mitosis, non-centrosomal MT nucleation is switched off (Borek et al., 2015) and the duplicated SPBs become the only active MTOCs, nucleating both intranuclear spindle MTs and cytoplasmic astral MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: During mitosis in fission yeast, the duplicated SPBs become the only active MTOCs, nucleating both intranuclear spindle MTs and cytoplasmic astral MTs.
source: As cells enter mitosis, non-centrosomal MT nucleation is switched off (Borek et al., 2015) and the duplicated SPBs become the only active MTOCs, nucleating both intranuclear spindle MTs and cytoplasmic astral MTs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Toward the end of cell division in fission yeast, microtubules are nucleated from the cytokinetic actomyosin ring (CAR).
source: Toward the end of cell division, microtubules are nucleated from the cytokinetic actomyosin ring (CAR).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about fission yeast.

claim: In budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the SPBs are the only MTOCs throughout the cell cycle.
source: By contrast, in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the SPBs are the only MTOCs throughout the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about budding yeast.

claim: In fission yeast, all types of MT nucleation in the cytoplasm depend on the Mto1/2 complex.
source: In fission yeast, all types of MT nucleation in the cytoplasm (i.e. both centrosomal and non-centrosomal nucleation) depend on the Mto1/2 complex (Janson et al., 2005; Samejima et al., 2005; Sawin et al., 2004; Venkatram et al., 2005; Venkatram et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mto1/2 contains multiple copies of the proteins Mto1 and Mto2.
source: Mto1/2 contains multiple copies of the proteins Mto1 and Mto2 and directly recruits the γ-tubulin complex to prospective MTOC sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Mto1/2 directly recruits the γ-tubulin complex to prospective MTOC sites.
source: Mto1/2 contains multiple copies of the proteins Mto1 and Mto2 and directly recruits the γ-tubulin complex to prospective MTOC sites.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: Mto1/2 interacts with the γ-tubulin complex via Mto1's Centrosomin Motif 1 (CM1) domain.
source: Mto1/2 interacts with the γ-tubulin complex via Mto1's Centrosomin Motif 1 (CM1) domain, which is conserved in higher eukaryotic MTOC regulators such as Drosophila centrosomin, and human CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin (Samejima et al., 2008; Sawin et al., 2004; Zhang and Megraw, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: The CM1 domain is conserved in higher eukaryotic MTOC regulators such as Drosophila centrosomin, and human CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin.
source: Mto1/2 interacts with the γ-tubulin complex via Mto1's Centrosomin Motif 1 (CM1) domain, which is conserved in higher eukaryotic MTOC regulators such as Drosophila centrosomin, and human CDK5RAP2 and myomegalin (Samejima et al., 2008; Sawin et al., 2004; Zhang and Megraw, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Interaction of CM1-domain proteins with the γ-tubulin complex can serve to activate the γ-tubulin complex.
source: Interaction of CM1-domain proteins with the γ-tubulin complex can also serve to activate the γ-tubulin complex (Choi et al., 2010; Lynch et al., 2014), although the detailed mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mto1/2 localizes to prospective MTOC sites independently of interacting with the γ-tubulin complex.
source: Because Mto1/2 localizes to prospective MTOC sites independently of interacting with the γ-tubulin complex (Samejima et al., 2008), Mto1/2 localization effectively determines where and when all cytoplasmic MTOCs are generated, and thus understanding Mto1/2 localization is critical to understanding MTOC formation more broadly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Mto1/2 localization effectively determines where and when all cytoplasmic MTOCs are generated.
source: Because Mto1/2 localizes to prospective MTOC sites independently of interacting with the γ-tubulin complex (Samejima et al., 2008), Mto1/2 localization effectively determines where and when all cytoplasmic MTOCs are generated, and thus understanding Mto1/2 localization is critical to understanding MTOC formation more broadly.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation and logical inference.

claim: Mto1/2 localization is mediated primarily by domains within Mto1.
source: Mto1/2 localization is mediated primarily by domains within Mto1 (Figure 1A; [Samejima et al., 2010]), although Mto2 contributes indirectly by helping to multimerize the Mto1/2 complex (Lynch et al., 2014; Samejima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Mto2 contributes indirectly to Mto1/2 localization by helping to multimerize the Mto1/2 complex.
source: Mto1/2 localization is mediated primarily by domains within Mto1 (Figure 1A; [Samejima et al., 2010]), although Mto2 contributes indirectly by helping to multimerize the Mto1/2 complex (Lynch et al., 2014; Samejima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mto1/2 association with pre-existing MTs depends on a broadly defined region near the Mto1 C-terminus.
source: Mto1/2 association with pre-existing MTs depends on a broadly defined region near the Mto1 C-terminus, while localization to the CAR and the SPB is mediated by overlapping modular sequences within the conserved MASC domain at the Mto1 C-terminus (Samejima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Localization of Mto1/2 to the CAR and the SPB is mediated by overlapping modular sequences within the conserved MASC domain at the Mto1 C-terminus.
source: Mto1/2 association with pre-existing MTs depends on a broadly defined region near the Mto1 C-terminus, while localization to the CAR and the SPB is mediated by overlapping modular sequences within the conserved MASC domain at the Mto1 C-terminus (Samejima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Localization of Mto1/2 to the CAR involves interaction of MASC with the unconventional myosin Myp2.
source: Localization to the CAR involves interaction of MASC with the unconventional myosin Myp2, while localization to the SPB involves the Septation Initiation Network protein Cdc11 (Samejima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Localization of Mto1/2 to the SPB involves the Septation Initiation Network protein Cdc11.
source: Localization to the CAR involves interaction of MASC with the unconventional myosin Myp2, while localization to the SPB involves the Septation Initiation Network protein Cdc11 (Samejima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to support the claim.

claim: Nuclear positioning was less accurate in mto1[bonsai]-GFP and mto1[∆130]-GFP cells compared to mto1[NE]-GFP and mto1-GFP cells.
source: Interestingly, nuclear positioning was less accurate in mto1[bonsai]-GFP and mto1[∆130]-GFP cells compared to mto1[NE]-GFP and mto1-GFP cells, indicating that MT nucleation from the NE contributes to nuclear positioning.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MT nucleation from the NE contributes to nuclear positioning.
source: Interestingly, nuclear positioning was less accurate in mto1[bonsai]-GFP and mto1[∆130]-GFP cells compared to mto1[NE]-GFP and mto1-GFP cells, indicating that MT nucleation from the NE contributes to nuclear positioning.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the nuclear positioning data.

claim: There was no difference in nuclear positioning between wild-type and mto1[NE] cells.
source: By contrast, there was no difference in nuclear positioning between wild-type and mto1[NE] cells, or between mto1[131–1115] and mto1[bonsai] cells, indicating that MT nucleation from the SPB is not particularly important for nuclear positioning.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MT nucleation from the SPB is not particularly important for nuclear positioning.
source: By contrast, there was no difference in nuclear positioning between wild-type and mto1[NE] cells, or between mto1[131–1115] and mto1[bonsai] cells, indicating that MT nucleation from the SPB is not particularly important for nuclear positioning.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the nuclear positioning data.

claim: Among the proteins significantly enriched in the Mto1[9A1-NE] interactome vs. the Mto1[9A1-bonsai] interactome, nucleoporin Nup146, exportin Crm1, the fission yeast TACC homolog Alp7, and polo kinase Plo1 were identified.
source: Among the proteins significantly enriched in the Mto1[9A1-NE] interactome vs. the Mto1[9A1-bonsai] interactome, we identified nucleoporin Nup146 (Asakawa et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2004), exportin Crm1 (Adachi and Yanagida, 1989; Fung and Chook, 2014; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007; Stade et al., 1997), the fission yeast TACC homolog, Alp7 (Sato et al., 2004), and, to a lesser extent, polo kinase Plo1 (Ohkura et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1F and Table 1.

claim: In alp7∆ deletion mutants, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP was present on the NE just as in wild-type (alp7+) cells.
source: However, we found that in alp7∆ deletion mutants, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP was present on the NE just as in wild-type (alp7+) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Alp7 is not required for Mto1 localization to the NE.
source: This indicates that Alp7 is not required for Mto1 localization to the NE.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Alp7 deletion data.

claim: Extensive colocalization of Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP with Nup146-3mCherry clusters was observed in nup132∆ cells.
source: We observed extensive colocalization of Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP with Nup146-3mCherry clusters (Figure 2A), indicating specific association with NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP specifically associates with NPCs.
source: We observed extensive colocalization of Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP with Nup146-3mCherry clusters (Figure 2A), indicating specific association with NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the colocalization data.

claim: Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localizes specifically at the cytoplasmic face of NPCs.
source: Consistent with this, we observed Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP specifically at the cytoplasmic face of NPCs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunoelectron microscopy data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Crm1 is the major transport receptor for nuclear export of proteins.
source: As the major transport receptor for nuclear export of proteins (as well as some RNAs), Crm1 normally forms a trimeric complex with export cargo and RanGTP within the nucleus, which facilitates transit of cargo through the permeability barrier of the NPC and into the cytoplasm (Dong et al., 2009; Fung and Chook, 2014; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Crm1 normally forms a trimeric complex with export cargo and RanGTP within the nucleus.
source: As the major transport receptor for nuclear export of proteins (as well as some RNAs), Crm1 normally forms a trimeric complex with export cargo and RanGTP within the nucleus, which facilitates transit of cargo through the permeability barrier of the NPC and into the cytoplasm (Dong et al., 2009; Fung and Chook, 2014; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: There is no evidence that Mto1 is ever present in the nucleus.
source: However, to date, there is no evidence that Mto1 is a nuclear export cargo or indeed is ever present in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about the lack of evidence.

claim: Nuclear export cargos typically bind to Crm1 via hydrophobic nuclear export signals (NESs).
source: Nuclear export cargos typically bind to Crm1 via hydrophobic nuclear export signals (NESs) (Dong et al., 2009; Fung and Chook, 2014; Fung et al., 2015; Güttler et al., 2010; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2007; Kutay and Güttinger, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Leptomycin B (LMB) inhibits Crm1 cargo-binding by binding within the hydrophobic NES-binding cleft of Crm1.
source: This can be inhibited by the drug leptomycin B (LMB), which binds within the hydrophobic NES-binding cleft of Crm1 (Dong et al., 2009; Fornerod et al., 1997a; Fukuda et al., 1997; Fung and Chook, 2014; Ossareh-Nazari et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: When cells are treated with LMB, nuclear export cargos accumulate within the nucleus.
source: As a result, when cells are treated with LMB, nuclear export cargos accumulate within the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as established knowledge about LMB effects.

claim: After LMB treatment, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP was lost from NPCs.
source: Interestingly, after LMB treatment, we found that Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP was lost from NPCs (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After LMB treatment, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP became dispersed in the cytoplasm rather than accumulating in the nucleus.
source: Strikingly, however, rather than accumulating in the nucleus, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP became dispersed in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After LMB treatment, Alp7-3GFP accumulated in the nucleoplasm and on an intranuclear MT bundle.
source: As expected, after LMB treatment, Alp7-3GFP accumulated in the nucleoplasm and on an intranuclear MT bundle that has been described to form upon LMB treatment of fission yeast (Matsuyama et al., 2006)(Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In crm1-C529A cells, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localized to NPCs both in the absence and in the presence of LMB.
source: Interestingly, we found that in crm1-C529A cells, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localized to NPCs both in the absence and in the presence of LMB (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of Mto1 from NPCs after LMB treatment can be specifically attributed to inhibition at the Crm1 cargo-binding cleft.
source: This demonstrates that loss of Mto1 from NPCs after LMB treatment can be specifically attributed to inhibition at the Crm1 cargo-binding cleft.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the crm1-C529A data.

claim: In control cells, MT regrowth after cold-shock occurred from the NE.
source: As expected, we found that in control cells, MT regrowth occurred from the NE.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In LMB-treated cells, MT regrowth after cold-shock occurred randomly in the cytoplasm.
source: However, in LMB-treated cells, MT regrowth occurred randomly in the cytoplasm, consistent with a failure of Mto1 to localize to the NE after LMB treatment (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only 3–4 out of nearly 500 quantified proteins were significantly enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from untreated cells compared to LMB-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, only 3–4 out of nearly 500 quantified proteins were significantly enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from untreated cells compared to LMB-treated cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C and Table 2.

claim: Crm1 showed the greatest enrichment (~20X) in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from untreated cells compared to LMB-treated cells.
source: Among these, Crm1 showed the greatest enrichment (~20X).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C and Table 2.

claim: Nup146 showed enrichment (~2.8X) in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from untreated cells compared to LMB-treated cells.
source: Nup146 also showed enrichment, but to a lesser extent (~2.8X), which may indicate that Mto1 can bind weakly to Nup146 independently of Crm1 (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3C and Table 2.

claim: Mto1 interaction with Crm1 requires Crm1 cargo-binding activity.
source: These results demonstrate that, like Mto1 localization to NPCs, Mto1 interaction with Crm1 requires Crm1 cargo-binding activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the LMB mass spectrometry data.

claim: The sequence spanning Mto1 amino acids 9–25 contained two closely overlapping candidate NESs.
source: The sequence spanning Mto1 amino acids 9–25 contained two closely overlapping candidate NESs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The spacing of hydrophobic amino acids within the Mto1 NES-like sequence is similar to that of several non-natural high-affinity NESs.
source: Interestingly, the spacing of hydrophobic amino acids within this NES-like sequence is similar to that of several non-natural high-affinity NESs (Figure 4B; [Engelsma et al., 2004; Güttler et al., 2010]).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: GFP-Mto1[∆NES-9A1-NE]-HTB failed to localize to NPCs and instead was present in the cytoplasm.
source: The truncated protein, termed GFP-Mto1[∆NES-9A1-NE]-HTB, failed to localize to NPCs and instead was present in the cytoplasm (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Very few proteins were enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome compared to GFP-Mto1[∆NES-9A1-NE]-HTB interactome.
source: As with LMB treatment, very few proteins were enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome compared to GFP-Mto1[∆NES-9A1-NE]-HTB interactome (Figure 4D; Table 3; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D and Table 3.

claim: Strong enrichment of both Crm1 (~85X) and Nup146 (~20X) was observed in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome compared to GFP-Mto1[∆NES-9A1-NE]-HTB interactome.
source: However, we observed strong enrichment of both Crm1 (~85X) and Nup146 (~20X).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D and Table 3.

claim: The importance of the Mto1 NES-like sequence both for localization to NPCs and for interaction with Crm1 strongly suggests that Mto1 is a direct but unconventional cargo for Crm1.
source: The importance of the Mto1 NES-like sequence both for localization to NPCs and for interaction with Crm1 strongly suggests that Mto1 is a direct but unconventional cargo for Crm1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the NES deletion data.

claim: GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST localized to puncta on the NE, which are interpreted to be NPCs.
source: Strikingly, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST localized to puncta on the NE, which we interpret to be NPCs (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: GFP-Mto1[1-12]-GST, which lacks the NES-M, did not show any specific localization.
source: By contrast, GFP-Mto1[1-12]-GST, which lacks the NES-M, did not show any specific localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: After LMB treatment, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was lost from NPCs.
source: We further found that after LMB treatment, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was lost from NPCs (Figure 4F); moreover, like Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was present exclusively in the cytoplasm after LMB treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was present exclusively in the cytoplasm after LMB treatment.
source: We further found that after LMB treatment, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was lost from NPCs (Figure 4F); moreover, like Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP, GFP-Mto1[1-29]-GST was present exclusively in the cytoplasm after LMB treatment.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GFP-Mto1[1-29]−13Myc did not localize to NPCs.
source: GFP-Mto1[1-29]−13Myc did not localize to NPCs (Figure 4E), suggesting that dimerization/multimerization may be an important factor for Mto1 NPC localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Dimerization/multimerization may be an important factor for Mto1 NPC localization.
source: GFP-Mto1[1-29]−13Myc did not localize to NPCs (Figure 4E), suggesting that dimerization/multimerization may be an important factor for Mto1 NPC localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the monomeric construct data.

claim: The Mto1 NES-M is both necessary and sufficient for localization to NPCs.
source: Collectively, these results indicate the Mto1 NES-M is both necessary and sufficient for localization to NPCs, without ever being present in the nucleus.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary interpretation of the NES experiments.

claim: Expression of spi1+ had no effect on Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localization.
source: Expression of spi1+ had no effect on Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of spi1[Q68L] did not alter Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localization to NPCs.
source: Expression of spi1[Q68L] impaired import of a nuclear localization signal (NLS) reporter protein, as expected (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but did not alter Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP localization to NPCs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of spi1[T23N] led to strong loss of Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP from NPCs.
source: Interestingly, expression of spi1[T23N], which had only minor effects on NLS reporter localization, led to strong loss of Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP from NPCs (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Mto1 localization to NPCs requires RanGTP.
source: These results indicate that, like nuclear export, Mto1 localization to NPCs requires RanGTP.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Ran mutant data.

claim: At least in the short-term, neither RanGDP nor Ran nucleotide cycling is required for Mto1 NPC localization.
source: Moreover, at least in the short-term, neither RanGDP nor Ran nucleotide cycling is required for Mto1 NPC localization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Ran mutant data.

claim: In nup146[∆FG5-12] cells, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP no longer localized to NPCs and instead was present only in the cytoplasm.
source: Strikingly, in nup146[∆FG5-12] cells, Mto1[9A1-NE]-GFP no longer localized to NPCs and instead was present only in the cytoplasm (Figure 6B; Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In wild-type cells, MT regrowth after cold-shock occurred from the NE, while in nup146[∆FG5-12] cells MT regrowth occurred randomly in the cytoplasm.
source: In wild-type cells, MT regrowth occurred from the NE, while in nup146[∆FG5-12] cells MT regrowth occurred randomly in the cytoplasm (Figure 6C), similar to LMB-treated wild-type cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In nup146[∆FG 5–12] cells, MT nucleation frequency in the vicinity of the NE was decreased by ~90% relative to wild-type (nup146+) cells.
source: In nup146[∆FG 5–12] cells, MT nucleation frequency in the vicinity of the NE was decreased by ~90% relative to wild-type (nup146+) cells, while nucleation frequency away from the NE was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Nucleation frequency away from the NE was unchanged in nup146[∆FG 5–12] cells compared to wild-type cells.
source: In nup146[∆FG 5–12] cells, MT nucleation frequency in the vicinity of the NE was decreased by ~90% relative to wild-type (nup146+) cells, while nucleation frequency away from the NE was unchanged.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live-cell imaging data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Nup146 FG repeats 5–12 are essential for Mto1 docking at the NPC.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Nup146 FG repeats 5–12 are essential for Mto1 docking at the NPC and, consequently, for MTOC nucleation from the NE.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Nup146 deletion data.

claim: Nup146 FG repeats 5–12 are essential for MTOC nucleation from the NE.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that Nup146 FG repeats 5–12 are essential for Mto1 docking at the NPC and, consequently, for MTOC nucleation from the NE.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Nup146 deletion data.

claim: This is the first biological function that can be uniquely attributed to the FG repeats of the Nup146/Sc Nup159/Hs Nup214 class of cytoplasmic FG-Nups, in any organism.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first biological function that can be uniquely attributed to the FG repeats of the Nup146/Sc Nup159/Hs Nup214 class of cytoplasmic FG-Nups, in any organism (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: A subset of FG repeats in Hs Nup214 have been shown to bind to Crm1 in a manner that stabilizes the Crm1-RanGTP-cargo interaction in vitro.
source: Interestingly, a subset of FG repeats in Hs Nup214 have been shown to bind to Crm1 in a manner that stabilizes the Crm1-RanGTP-cargo interaction in vitro (Askjaer et al., 1999; Fornerod et al., 1997b; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2006; Kehlenbach et al., 1999; Port et al., 2015; Roloff et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Among more than 500 quantified proteins, only five to six proteins were significantly enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from nup146+ cells compared to nup146[∆FG5-12] cells.
source: Among more than 500 quantified proteins, only five to six proteins were significantly enriched in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from nup146+ cells compared to nup146[∆FG5-12] cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6F and Table 4.

claim: Nup146 itself showed the greatest enrichment (~11X) in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from nup146+ cells compared to nup146[∆FG5-12] cells.
source: Nup146 itself showed the greatest enrichment (~11X), while Crm1 was also enriched, although to a lesser extent (~3X) (Figure 6F; Table 4; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6F and Table 4.

claim: Crm1 was enriched (~3X) in the GFP-Mto1[9A1-NE]-HTB interactome from nup146+ cells compared to nup146[∆FG5-12] cells.
source: Nup146 itself showed the greatest enrichment (~11X), while Crm1 was also enriched, although to a lesser extent (~3X) (Figure 6F; Table 4; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 6F and Table 4.

claim: Nup146 FG repeats are essential for interaction of Mto1 with Nup146.
source: This suggests that Nup146 FG repeats are essential for interaction of Mto1 with Nup146.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Nup146 deletion mass spectrometry data.

claim: While Nup146 FG repeats may not be absolutely essential for formation of an Mto1-Crm1 complex, they may help to stabilize it.
source: In addition, while Nup146 FG repeats may not be absolutely essential for formation of an Mto1-Crm1 complex, they may help to stabilize it.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the Nup146 deletion mass spectrometry data.

claim: The mechanism described for Mto1 localization to NPCs was entirely unexpected.
source: The mechanism described here for Mto1 localization to NPCs was entirely unexpected.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a characterization of the findings.

claim: When not interacting with the export machinery, Mto1 (and its partner Mto2) is a cytoplasmic protein rather than a nuclear protein.
source: First, when not interacting with the export machinery, Mto1(and its partner Mto2) is a cytoplasmic protein rather than a nuclear protein.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key distinction from conventional export.

claim: Interaction of Mto1 with the export machinery leads to docking at NPCs, rather than a return/release into the cytoplasm.
source: Second, interaction of Mto1 with the export machinery leads to docking at NPCs, rather than a return/release into the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key distinction from conventional export.

claim: This is the first example of a nuclear export-like complex being used to dock a cytoplasmic 'cargo' at the NPC, with no obvious functional link to export.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of a nuclear export-like complex being used to dock a cytoplasmic 'cargo' at the NPC, with no obvious functional link to export.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Nuclear transport receptors and nucleoporins are known to have non-transport-related roles away from NPCs, especially in relation to mitosis and microtubule function.
source: Nuclear transport receptors and nucleoporins are known to have non-transport-related roles away from NPCs, especially in relation to mitosis and microtubule function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: In many cell types, importins play a major role in RanGTP-dependent regulation of mitotic spindle assembly factors.
source: In many cell types, importins play a major role in RanGTP-dependent regulation of mitotic spindle assembly factors, while Crm1 has been described to have roles both at centrosomes and kinetochores (reviewed in (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015; Forbes et al., 2015; Kalab and Heald, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Crm1 has been described to have roles both at centrosomes and kinetochores.
source: In many cell types, importins play a major role in RanGTP-dependent regulation of mitotic spindle assembly factors, while Crm1 has been described to have roles both at centrosomes and kinetochores (reviewed in (Cavazza and Vernos, 2015; Forbes et al., 2015; Kalab and Heald, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In mammalian cells, Crm1 is involved in RanGTP-dependent kinetochore targeting of a complex containing RanGAP1 and RanBP2.
source: In particular, in mammalian cells, Crm1 is involved in RanGTP-dependent kinetochore targeting of a complex containing RanGAP1 and RanBP2 (a metazoan-specific cytoplasmic FG-Nup, also known as Nup358,), and this is important for the integrity of kinetochore microtubules (Arnaoutov et al., 2005), perhaps because of the SUMO E3 ligase activity of RanBP2 (Ritterhoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Crm1-dependent kinetochore targeting of RanGAP1/RanBP2 is important for the integrity of kinetochore microtubules.
source: In particular, in mammalian cells, Crm1 is involved in RanGTP-dependent kinetochore targeting of a complex containing RanGAP1 and RanBP2 (a metazoan-specific cytoplasmic FG-Nup, also known as Nup358,), and this is important for the integrity of kinetochore microtubules (Arnaoutov et al., 2005), perhaps because of the SUMO E3 ligase activity of RanBP2 (Ritterhoff et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In Crm1-dependent targeting of RanGAP1/RanBP2 to kinetochores, the Crm1 'cargo' remains unknown.
source: In Crm1-dependent targeting of RanGAP1/RanBP2 to kinetochores, the Crm1 'cargo' remains unknown, and the mechanism by which Crm1 associates with kinetochores appears to be controversial (Platani et al., 2009; Zuccolo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In many cell types, the multi-protein Nup107-160 complex is recruited to kinetochores, where it may promote MT nucleation by the γ-tubulin complex.
source: In many cell types, the multi-protein Nup107-160 complex (also known as Y complex; [Kabachinski and Schwartz, 2015]) is also recruited to kinetochores, where it may promote MT nucleation by the γ-tubulin complex (Mishra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Recruitment of the Nup107-160 complex to kinetochores depends on RanGTP.
source: This process also depends on RanGTP, but any specific role for nuclear transport receptors here remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as established knowledge.

claim: In human cells, cargo containing a non-natural, high-affinity NES was shown to accumulate at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC and also to enhance Crm1 accumulation at the same site.
source: Interestingly, in human cells, cargo containing a non-natural, high-affinity NES (a 'supraphysiological NES') was shown to accumulate at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC and also to enhance Crm1 accumulation at the same site (Engelsma et al., 2004; Engelsma et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The Mto1 NES-M may be a natural high-affinity NES.
source: We hypothesize that the Mto1 NES-M may be a natural high-affinity NES.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on the data.

claim: Several high-affinity NESs depend on a fifth hydrophobic residue, which may also be present in the Mto1 NES-M.
source: In particular, relative to an original consensus involving four spaced hydrophobic residues (Kutay and Güttinger, 2005), several high-affinity NESs depend on a fifth hydrophobic residue, which may also be present in the Mto1 NES-M (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation and reference to Figure 4B.

claim: Crm1 can exist in two conformations: an unliganded extended, superhelical conformation, and a compact, ring-like conformation.
source: Crm1 can exist in two conformations: an unliganded extended, superhelical conformation, which is inhibitory to cargo and RanGTP binding, and a compact, ring-like conformation, which is stabilized by cooperative binding to cargo and RanGTP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: The FG-repeat fragment of Hs Nup214 interacts with the compact conformation of Crm1 at multiple sites, spanning the junction between the Crm1 N- and C-termini.
source: Importantly, the FG-repeat fragment of Hs Nup214, which binds Crm1 cooperatively with RanGTP and cargo, interacts with the compact conformation of Crm1 at multiple sites, spanning the junction between the Crm1 N- and C-termini in a manner similar to an adhesive bandage (Port et al., 2015) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation and reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Hs Nup214 FG repeats have been described as a 'molecular clamp' that can stabilize Crm1-RanGTP-cargo complex in the compact conformation.
source: The Hs Nup214 FG repeats have therefore been described as a 'molecular clamp' that can stabilize Crm1-RanGTP-cargo complex in the compact conformation (Port et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: A sufficiently high-affinity NES cargo would be expected to stabilize interaction of Crm1 with Nup146, leading to docking of Crm1 (and the NES cargo itself) at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC.
source: As a result, a sufficiently high-affinity NES cargo would be expected to stabilize interaction of Crm1 with Nup146, leading to docking of Crm1 (and the NES cargo itself) at the cytoplasmic face of the NPC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis based on structural knowledge.

claim: Mto1/2 is multimeric in vivo, containing multiple (>10) copies of both Mto1 and Mto2.
source: Mto1/2 is multimeric in vivo, containing multiple (>10) copies of both Mto1 and Mto2 (Lynch et al., 2014), while nucleoporins are also present in multiple copies within the NPC, because of its eight-fold symmetry (Aitchison and Rout, 2012; Görlich and Kutay, 1999; Wente and Rout, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Nucleoporins are present in multiple copies within the NPC, because of its eight-fold symmetry.
source: Mto1/2 is multimeric in vivo, containing multiple (>10) copies of both Mto1 and Mto2 (Lynch et al., 2014), while nucleoporins are also present in multiple copies within the NPC, because of its eight-fold symmetry (Aitchison and Rout, 2012; Görlich and Kutay, 1999; Wente and Rout, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Localization of Mto1/2 to the SPB and the CAR depends on avidity effects.
source: Interestingly, localization of Mto1/2 to the SPB and the CAR also depends on avidity effects (Samejima et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to support the claim.

claim: In yeast, RanGAP is freely soluble in the cytoplasm rather than associated with the NPC.
source: While the low concentration of RanGTP in the cytoplasm makes this unlikely, it is formally possible that in the immediate vicinity of the NPC, the local concentration of RanGTP is higher than in the cytoplasm in general, because in yeast, RanGAP is freely soluble in the cytoplasm rather than associated with the NPC (Aitchison and Rout, 2012; Hopper et al., 1990).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Extensive analysis in budding yeast has shown that the FG regions of cytoplasmic FG-Nups can be deleted without almost any discernible effects on nuclear transport.
source: In this context, it is interesting that extensive analysis in budding yeast has shown that the FG regions of cytoplasmic FG-Nups (as well as nucleoplasmic FG-Nups) can be deleted without almost any discernible effects on nuclear transport (Adams et al., 2014; Strawn et al., 2004; Zeitler and Weis, 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: In at least one instance where Hs Nup214 was found to be important for export of the 60S pre-ribosome, the FG repeats of Hs Nup214 were found not to be required.
source: In human cells, the role of Hs Nup214 in protein export appears to be somewhat controversial (Bernad et al., 2006; Hutten and Kehlenbach, 2006); however, similar to budding yeast, in at least one instance where Hs Nup214 was found to be important for export—namely, export of the 60S pre-ribosome— the FG repeats of Hs Nup214 were found not to be required [Bernad et al., 2006]).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support the claim.

claim: An important but previously unrecognized role for cytoplasmic FG-Nups may be to dock cytoplasmic proteins at the NPC for non-export-related functions.
source: Based on these results, and on the conservation of FG repeats in Nup146, Sc Nup159 and Hs Nup214, we propose that an important but previously unrecognized role for cytoplasmic FG-Nups may be to dock cytoplasmic proteins at the NPC for non-export-related functions, as described here for generation of non-centrosomal MTOCs by the Mto1/2 complex.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal based on the findings.
